narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and only accepts students with a strong likelihood of passing, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your class ranking after the third year of law school, your first-year class ranking, and your LSAT score. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of accepted students. This was the single most important reason the model saw a high risk of bar failure. Your first-year ranking was also in the bottom decile, compared with an average around the middle of the class for accepted applicants; this gave the prediction another substantial push toward rejection. Finally, your LSAT score of 27 sits well below the average of 37 for students who were admitted, adding further weight to the concern that you would struggle to pass the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5, also noticeably below the accepted average of 3.23, and your middle family income bracket (typical among accepted students) played smaller roles. The fact that you plan to attend full-time aligned with the vast majority of successful applicants and did not hurt your chances.

To improve your prospects, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining law school years, consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score, and explore bar-preparation resources early. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to this decision. (248 words)
